title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Natasha opened Prince Andrew's door with the ease of long habit and let Princess Mary go into the room ahead of her. The princess felt sobs rising in her throat. She had tried hard to prepare herself, and she was trying now to stay calm, but she knew she could not look at him without tears.

The princess understood what Natasha had meant by "two days ago this suddenly happened." It meant that he had suddenly grown softer, and that this softness and gentleness were signs that death was near. As she walked to the door she could already picture Andrew's face as she remembered it from childhood: gentle, mild, sympathetic, a face he had rarely shown, and so one that moved her all the more. She was sure he would say soft, tender things to her, as her father had before he died, and that she would not be able to bear it and would burst into sobs in front of him. But sooner or later it had to happen, and she went in. The sobs rose higher and higher in her throat as his figure became clearer and her shortsighted eyes tried to make out his features. Then she saw his face and met his gaze.

He was lying on a divan in a squirrel-fur dressing gown, propped up with pillows. He was thin and pale. In one thin hand, so white it was almost translucent, he held a handkerchief; with the other he slowly stroked the fine mustache he had grown, moving his fingers gently. His eyes were fixed on them as they came in.

The moment she saw his face and met his eyes, Princess Mary's steps slowed. Her tears dried up and her sobs stopped. Seeing the expression in his face and eyes, she suddenly felt guilty and grew timid.
"But what am I to blame for?" she asked herself. And his cold, stern look answered: "For being alive and thinking of the living, while I..."
His gaze was deep, and seemed to look not outward but inward. As he slowly regarded his sister and Natasha, there was something almost hostile in it.
He kissed his sister, keeping her hand in his, as they always used to do.
"How are you, Mary? How did you ever get here?" he said, in a voice as calm and distant as his look.
If he had screamed in agony, the scream would not have horrified Princess Mary as much as the tone of his voice did.
"And did you bring little Nicholas?" he asked in the same slow, quiet way, plainly making an effort to remember.
"How are you now?" said Princess Mary, surprised at her own words.
"You must ask the doctor that, my dear," he replied. Again he made an obvious effort to be affectionate, and said, with his lips only (his words clearly did not match his thoughts):
"Merci, chère amie, d'être venue." *
* "Thank you for coming, my dear."

Princess Mary pressed his hand. He winced, just barely, at the pressure. He said nothing, and she did not know what to say. Now she understood what had happened to him two days before. In his words, in his tone, and above all in that calm, almost antagonistic look, she could feel a detachment from everything of this world, terrible in someone still alive. He plainly understood anything living only with effort. But it was obvious that he failed to understand, not because he lacked the ability, but because he understood something else, something the living did not and could not understand, and it filled his mind completely.
"There, you see how strangely fate has brought us together," he said, breaking the silence and pointing at Natasha. "She takes care of me all the time."

Princess Mary heard him and could not understand how he could say such a thing. He was sensitive, tender Prince Andrew. How could he say that, in front of the woman he loved and who loved him? If he had expected to live, he could not have said those words in that offensively cold tone. If he had not known he was dying, how could he fail to pity her, and how could he speak like that in her presence? The only explanation was that he was indifferent, because something else, far more important, had been revealed to him.
The conversation was cold and disjointed, and kept breaking off.
"Mary came by way of Ryazan," said Natasha.
Prince Andrew did not notice that she called his sister Mary. Natasha herself noticed it only after she had said it in his presence.
"Did she?" he asked.
"They told her all of Moscow has burned down, and that..."
Natasha stopped. Talking was impossible. It was plain that he was trying to listen but could not.
"Yes, they say it's burned," he said. "That's a great pity," and he stared straight ahead, absently stroking his mustache with his fingers.

"So you've met Count Nicholas, Mary?" Prince Andrew said suddenly, evidently wanting to say something pleasant to them. "He wrote here that he took a great liking to you," he went on, simply and calmly, evidently unable to grasp how much his words would mean to the living. "If you liked him too, it would be a good thing for you to marry," he added, a little more quickly, as if glad to have found words he had long been looking for.
Princess Mary heard his words, but they meant nothing to her except as proof of how far he now was from everything living.
"Why talk about me?" she said quietly, and glanced at Natasha.
Natasha felt her glance but did not look at her. All three were silent again.
"Andrew, would you like..." Princess Mary said suddenly, in a trembling voice, "would you like to see little Nicholas? He's always talking about you!"

Prince Andrew smiled, barely, and for the first time. But Princess Mary, who knew his face so well, saw with horror that it was not a smile of pleasure or of love for his son. It was a quiet, gentle irony, because he thought she was trying what she took to be the last means of rousing him.
"Yes, I'll be very glad to see him. Is he quite well?"

When little Nicholas was brought into Prince Andrew's room, he looked at his father with frightened eyes but did not cry, because no one else was crying. Prince Andrew kissed him and evidently did not know what to say to him.
After Nicholas had been led away, Princess Mary went up to her brother again and kissed him. She could no longer hold back her tears, and she began to cry.
He looked at her intently.
"Is it about Nicholas?" he asked.
Princess Mary nodded, weeping.
"Mary, you know the Gosp..." but he broke off.
"What did you say?"
"Nothing. You mustn't cry here," he said, looking at her with the same cold expression.

When Princess Mary began to cry, he understood that she was crying at the thought that little Nicholas would be left without a father. With a great effort he tried to come back to life and see things as they saw them.
"Yes, to them it must seem sad!" he thought. "But how simple it is.

"The fowls of the air sow not, neither do they reap, yet your Father feedeth them," he said to himself, and wanted to say it to Princess Mary. "But no, they'll take it their own way, they won't understand! They can't understand that all those feelings they prize so much, all our feelings, all those ideas that seem so important to us, are unnecessary. We cannot understand one another," and he stayed silent.

Prince Andrew's little son was seven. He could barely read, and he knew nothing. After that day he lived through many things and gained knowledge, observation and experience. But even if he had had all the faculties he later acquired, he could not have understood the meaning of the scene he had witnessed between his father, Mary and Natasha any better or more deeply than he did then. He understood it completely. He left the room without crying and went silently to Natasha, who had come out with him. He looked shyly at her with his beautiful, thoughtful eyes. Then his raised, rosy upper lip trembled, and he leaned his head against her and began to cry.

After that he avoided Dessalles and the countess, who caressed him. He either sat alone or came timidly to Princess Mary, or to Natasha, of whom he seemed even fonder than of his aunt, and clung to them quietly and shyly.

When Princess Mary left Prince Andrew, she understood fully what Natasha's face had told her. She did not speak to Natasha again about hopes of saving his life. She took turns with her beside his sofa. She no longer cried, but prayed continually, turning in her soul to that Eternal and Unfathomable One, whose presence above the dying man was now so evident.
